summary: Clifford Brown was a trumpeter whose warm tone and fluent, clean lines made him the model hard bop trumpeter of the 1950s. His quintet with Max Roach set the standard for the style.
know: He co-led the Clifford Brown–Max Roach Quintet, one of the defining hard bop bands.
He wrote the standards Joy Spring and Daahoud.
His recording career lasted only about four years.

influencedBy.why: Brown built his fast, harmonically sharp bebop vocabulary on Gillespie's trumpet language.
Roach was his co-leader and drummer, and the two shaped the quintet's sound together.
Brown played in Blakey's early band on the live A Night at Birdland sessions in 1954.

influenced.why: Rollins joined the Brown–Roach Quintet in 1955 and developed his hard bop playing beside Brown.

cousins.why: A short, hugely influential career that set a template for players who followed.
The same smooth, effortless phrasing that sounds easy but is very hard to copy.

summary: Gil Evans was an arranger and bandleader who brought orchestral color and space to jazz. His albums with Miles Davis are some of the most admired large-ensemble jazz records.
know: His small apartment in Manhattan was a meeting place for the musicians who made Birth of the Cool.
He arranged Miles Ahead, Porgy and Bess and Sketches of Spain for Miles Davis.
He used French horns and tuba in jazz settings, which was unusual at the time.

influencedBy.why: Evans learned from Ellington how to write for individual voices and tone colors in a band.
Evans often named Armstrong as an early inspiration and an example of melodic freedom.
Evans arranged bebop themes and hosted Parker, and adapted bebop lines into orchestral writing.
His lush, impressionistic voicings follow the path Strayhorn opened in the Ellington band.

influenced.why: Evans arranged Davis's great orchestral albums and was one of his closest musical partners.
Mulligan was part of the circle that met at Evans's apartment and wrote for the Birth of the Cool nonet.

cousins.why: An arranger who used orchestral color to shape a star's records.
A big-picture arranger and producer who set the sound around a featured artist.

summary: Chet Baker was a trumpeter and singer whose soft, lyrical sound became the face of West Coast cool jazz. His quiet, close-mic singing shaped how later singers approached a ballad.
know: He first became known in Gerry Mulligan's pianoless quartet.
Chet Baker Sings made his voice as famous as his trumpet.
He played the trumpet solo on Elvis Costello's Shipbuilding in 1983.
songs: I Fall in Love Too Easily

influencedBy.why: Baker's spare, middle-register trumpet followed the cool approach Davis was developing.
Baker's early fame came in Mulligan's quartet, where he learned to play lyrical counterpoint.
Parker hired him for West Coast dates in 1952, an early break for Baker.
His clear, lyrical, understated tone is often traced back to Beiderbecke's cornet style.

influenced.why: Gilberto's hushed bossa nova singing is widely linked to the soft vocal style of Chet Baker Sings.
Veloso has named Baker's singing as part of the cool sound that shaped him.
Her calm, unforced delivery follows the same quiet approach Baker made popular.
Costello sought Baker out to play the trumpet solo on Shipbuilding.

cousins.why: Soft, intimate singing that pulls the listener in close.
Hushed, melancholy delivery with a fragile beauty.

summary: Gerry Mulligan was a baritone saxophonist, composer and arranger who helped define cool jazz. His pianoless quartet with Chet Baker showed how much space and counterpoint a small group could use.
know: He wrote and arranged several pieces for Miles Davis's Birth of the Cool sessions.
His 1952 quartet with Chet Baker had no piano, so the horns carried the harmony.
He made the baritone sax a lead instrument rather than a background one.

influencedBy.why: Mulligan's light, airy tone and relaxed swing follow Young's tenor approach.
Evans was his mentor in arranging and the center of the Birth of the Cool circle.
Mulligan wrote for and played in Davis's nonet, the core of the cool style.
His swinging, riff-based writing draws on the Basie band's economy.

influenced.why: Baker came to fame in Mulligan's quartet, learning to play melodic counterpoint with him.
Piazzolla's Octeto Buenos Aires drew on Mulligan's cool jazz groups, and the two later recorded Summit together.

cousins.why: Two voices weaving around each other in close counterpoint.
Sophisticated arrangements and cool, controlled musicianship.

summary: Stan Getz was a tenor saxophonist famous for his smooth, light tone. His collaborations with João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim brought bossa nova to a worldwide audience.
know: He played in Woody Herman's band in the late 1940s and was nicknamed The Sound.
Jazz Samba with Charlie Byrd started the American bossa nova boom.
Getz/Gilberto won the Grammy for Album of the Year.

influencedBy.why: Getz named Young as his main model for a light, floating tenor tone.
His fast bebop lines in the late 1940s came from Parker's language.
Gilberto's guitar and voice set the rhythmic feel Getz played over on Getz/Gilberto.
Jobim wrote and played the songs that defined Getz's bossa nova records.

influenced.why: Her first recording was the vocal on Getz/Gilberto, which made her a star.
Getz hired the young Silver in 1950, giving him his first big break.

cousins.why: Smooth, quiet sophistication with a cool, steady glow.
Gentle tone and understatement that rewards close listening.

summary: Cannonball Adderley was an alto saxophonist with a joyful, blues-soaked sound. He played on Kind of Blue and then led one of the most popular soul jazz bands of the 1960s.
know: He caused a stir sitting in at a New York club in 1955 while still a high school band teacher in Florida.
He was a member of Miles Davis's sextet on Milestones and Kind of Blue.
His quintet had a pop hit with Mercy, Mercy, Mercy in 1966.
keyAlbums: The Cannonball Adderley Quintet in San Francisco
Mercy, Mercy, Mercy! Live at "The Club"

influencedBy.why: Adderley's quick, fluent alto lines grew directly from Parker's style.
Playing in Davis's sextet pushed him toward modal ideas and space.
He shared the front line with Coltrane in the Davis sextet and the two pushed each other.

influenced.why: Joe Zawinul spent about nine years in Adderley's band, writing Mercy, Mercy, Mercy, before co-founding Weather Report.

cousins.why: Warm, gospel-tinged instrumental grooves with broad appeal.
Tight, bluesy groove music built for a live crowd.

summary: Horace Silver was a pianist and composer who helped invent hard bop by mixing bebop with blues and gospel feeling. His catchy, groove-based tunes became jazz standards.
know: He co-founded the Jazz Messengers with Art Blakey.
Song for My Father drew on his father's Cape Verdean musical heritage.
He spent nearly three decades on Blue Note Records.
keyAlbums: Horace Silver and the Jazz Messengers

influencedBy.why: Silver built his bebop piano technique on Powell's model.
His percussive, spare comping shows Monk's influence.
Blakey was his co-founder and drummer in the first Jazz Messengers.
Getz hired him in 1950 and brought him to New York.

influenced.why: Rikki Don't Lose That Number opens with a bass line borrowed from Song for My Father.

cousins.why: Gospel and blues feeling poured into a modern form.
Catchy, groove-first instrumentals built on repeated figures.

summary: The Delmore Brothers, Alton and Rabon, were a harmony duo who blended country, blues and boogie. Their close harmonies and boogie rhythms pointed toward rockabilly and the great brother duos.
know: They were early stars of the Grand Ole Opry in the 1930s.
Rabon played a four-string tenor guitar, which gave them a distinct sound.
Their late 1940s King Records sides like Freight Train Boogie are often called early rock and roll.
songs: Gonna Lay Down My Old Guitar

influencedBy.why: Their blues-tinged country songs follow the path Rodgers opened.
Their old-time repertoire and harmony singing share roots with the Carter Family's songs.
Macon was an Opry star they worked alongside early in their career.

influenced.why: The Everlys cited the Delmores as a model for brother harmony singing.
The Louvins built on the Delmores' close-harmony duet style.
Watson recorded Delmore songs and carried their style into the folk revival.
Travis sang with them in the gospel group the Brown's Ferry Four.

cousins.why: Tight family harmonies that made a small group sound full.
Two voices locked in close harmony.

summary: Merle Travis was a singer, songwriter and guitarist whose thumb-picking style became known as Travis picking. He wrote Sixteen Tons and Dark as a Dungeon about life in Kentucky coal country.
know: Travis picking, a thumb-and-finger style, is named after him.
He helped design an early solid-body electric guitar with Paul Bigsby in the late 1940s.
He appeared on the 1972 album Will the Circle Be Unbroken.

influencedBy.why: He sang with the Delmores in the Brown's Ferry Four and shared their country-blues blend.
His bluesy country songwriting follows Rodgers's example.

influenced.why: Atkins said hearing Travis on the radio shaped his own fingerpicking style.
Watson admired Travis so much he named his son Merle.
They invited Travis to play on Will the Circle Be Unbroken.
Reed's thumb-driven picking builds on the Travis style.

cousins.why: A self-taught thumb-picking style with a steady alternating bass.
Gentle, rolling fingerpicking with the bass on the thumb.

summary: The Stanley Brothers, Carter and Ralph, were among the first groups to follow Bill Monroe's bluegrass model. They kept bluegrass close to the older mountain sound, with high, lonesome harmonies.
know: They became popular on the Farm and Fun Time radio show in Bristol.
Carter wrote most of their songs and sang lead, with Ralph singing tenor.
Their version of Man of Constant Sorrow helped make it a standard.

influencedBy.why: They built their band on Monroe's bluegrass sound, and Carter briefly played with Monroe.
Their mountain repertoire and family harmony echo the Carter Family.

influenced.why: Ralph carried the brothers' sound into his long solo career with the Clinch Mountain Boys.
Skaggs learned by copying Stanley Brothers records and later played with Ralph.
Dylan often named them among his favorites and recorded Rank Strangers to Me.
Welch's stark harmonies follow the high lonesome Stanley sound.
Their string band revival draws on Stanley Brothers material and style.

cousins.why: Family harmonies rooted in church singing.
Raw, lonesome Appalachian music.

summary: Dock Boggs was a banjo player and singer from the Virginia coalfields whose dark, bluesy recordings stand apart from most old-time music. His songs on Harry Smith's Anthology made him a touchstone for the folk revival.
know: He recorded a handful of sides in 1927 and 1929, then stopped performing for decades.
Mike Seeger found him in 1963 and recorded him again for Folkways.
He played banjo with a bluesy, two-finger style learned partly from Black musicians in his area.

influenced.why: Dylan has praised Boggs, and writers often tie his darker folk material to Boggs's recordings.
Welch's stark, minor-key Appalachian songs follow the mood Boggs's records set.

cousins.why: Eerie, minor-key 1920s recordings by a player rediscovered in the 1960s.
A small set of intense early recordings that later players treat as essential.

summary: Alan Lomax was a folklorist and field recordist who documented American and world folk music for decades. His recordings gave the first hearing to many blues and folk musicians and fed the folk revival.
know: He began recording with his father, John Lomax, for the Library of Congress in the 1930s.
He made the first recordings of Muddy Waters in Mississippi in 1941.
He recorded long interviews with Jelly Roll Morton about early jazz in 1938.
keyAlbums: The Library of Congress Recordings (Jelly Roll Morton)

influencedBy.why: Working with Lead Belly in the 1930s showed Lomax what a living tradition could sound like.
His sessions with Morton shaped his idea of recording musicians telling their own history.
Lomax recorded and promoted Guthrie, and Guthrie shaped his view of topical folk song.

influenced.why: Lomax made Muddy's first recordings, and Muddy said hearing them convinced him he could make it.
Lomax recorded House in 1941 and 1942, preserving his playing from that era.
Lomax recorded and promoted Lead Belly, bringing him to New York audiences.
His 1940 Library of Congress sessions documented Guthrie's songs and stories.
The 1938 sessions are a main source for Morton's music and history.
Lomax hired the young Seeger at the Archive of American Folk Song.
Moby's album Play is built on samples of Lomax field recordings, including Natural Blues.

cousins.why: A recordist whose work captured a whole genre's key players.
Put southern blues voices on record and into wide circulation.

summary: Harry Smith was a collector and artist who assembled the Anthology of American Folk Music from his 78 rpm records. The set reintroduced 1920s and 1930s country and blues recordings and became a blueprint for the folk revival.
know: The Anthology was released by Folkways in 1952 as six LPs in three volumes.
He arranged the tracks by theme, not by race or region, mixing blues and country side by side.
He was also an experimental filmmaker and painter.
keyAlbums: Anthology of American Folk Music, Vol. 4

influencedBy.why: The Carter Family's records were among the central tracks Smith chose.
Smith included Boggs's recordings, which became some of the Anthology's best known.
Hurt's 1928 sides were part of Smith's collection and the Anthology.
Smith included Johnson's gospel blues on the Anthology.
Macon's banjo songs were part of the old-time core of the Anthology.
Smith included Patton's Delta blues in the set.

influenced.why: Dylan learned many songs from the Anthology, and its repertoire runs through his folk work.
Van Ronk described the Anthology as a central text for the Greenwich Village folk scene.
Jerry Garcia learned old-time and jug band material from the Anthology.
Welch's songwriting draws on the old-time world the Anthology preserved.

cousins.why: A crate digger who built new art from old records.
Collage made from forgotten recordings, arranged to tell a story.

summary: Josh White was a guitarist and singer who moved from Carolina blues into the New York folk and cabaret scene. He was one of the first Black folk and blues artists to reach a wide white audience.
know: As a boy he worked as a guide for traveling blind street singers.
He was a featured performer at the Café Society club in New York in the 1940s.
His albums Chain Gang and Southern Exposure were early protest records.
songs: Jesus Gonna Make Up My Dying Bed

influencedBy.why: White and Lead Belly performed together in the New York folk scene and shared material.
His clean Piedmont fingerpicking sits in the same Southeast blues tradition as McTell.

influenced.why: Van Ronk cited White's guitar playing and arrangements as a model.
White's polished folk act in New York clubs set an example for Belafonte's folk career.
White's 1950s tours of Britain helped spread the folk blues that fed skiffle.
White's recorded version of House of the Rising Sun is part of the chain that led to theirs.

cousins.why: A singer who crossed from church and roots music into polished nightclub appeal.
Smooth crossover star who reached a mainstream audience with grace.

summary: Elizabeth Cotten was a self-taught guitarist who played left-handed on a guitar strung for a right-handed player. Her song Freight Train became a folk standard, and her style is now called Cotten picking.
know: She wrote Freight Train as a young girl in North Carolina.
She was working for the Seeger family when they discovered her playing.
She won a Grammy in 1985 for Elizabeth Cotten Live!
songs: Oh Babe It Ain't No Lie

influenced.why: The Seeger family recorded and promoted her, and her songs entered the revival repertoire through them.
They recorded Freight Train, spreading it to a large audience.
Jerry Garcia played Oh Babe It Ain't No Lie and other Cotten songs.

cousins.why: Gentle fingerpicking and a late-life discovery that won over the folk revival.
A thumb-picking guitar style so personal it carries the player's name.

summary: Harry Belafonte was a singer and actor who brought Caribbean calypso and folk songs to a mass audience. His album Calypso was a huge seller and made him one of the biggest stars of the 1950s.
know: Calypso was the first album by a single artist to sell over a million copies in the US, according to many accounts.
He helped bring Miriam Makeba to American audiences.
Bob Dylan's first professional recording was playing harmonica on a Belafonte album.

influencedBy.why: Belafonte recorded Lead Belly songs and credited him as an influence on his folk repertoire.
Guthrie's folk songs were part of the material Belafonte drew on early on.
White's polished folk club act was a model for Belafonte's early folk performances.

influenced.why: Belafonte's calypso and folk hits opened the market the Kingston Trio broke into.
Belafonte mentored Makeba and they won a Grammy together for An Evening with Belafonte/Makeba.
Belafonte helped Masekela come to the US and start his career there.
Dylan played harmonica on Belafonte's Midnight Special in 1962.

cousins.why: Caribbean music carried to a worldwide audience by a charismatic voice.
Jamaican pop with an easy, sing-along appeal that crossed borders.

summary: The Ink Spots were a vocal group whose slow ballads set the template for doo-wop and R&B vocal groups. Their formula of a high tenor lead and a spoken bass part was copied for decades.
know: Bill Kenny's high tenor and Hoppy Jones's spoken bass were their trademarks.
If I Didn't Care in 1939 became one of the best selling records of its era.
They recorded Into Each Life Some Rain Must Fall with Ella Fitzgerald.
songs: I Don't Want to Set the World on Fire
Into Each Life Some Rain Must Fall

influencedBy.why: The Mills Brothers had already shown a Black vocal group could top the pop charts with smooth harmony.

influenced.why: The Orioles built their ballad style on the Ink Spots' tenor-led sound.
The Platters' slow, dramatic ballads follow the Ink Spots' model.
Early R&B groups like the Dominoes used the Ink Spots' lead and bass layout.
Elvis's first home recording at Sun included the Ink Spots' That's When Your Heartaches Begin.

cousins.why: High tenor harmony with a sad, sweet edge.
Close harmony ballads that set a template for later groups.

summary: The Mills Brothers were a family vocal group known for imitating instruments with their voices. They were among the first Black performers with national radio shows and had hits across five decades.
know: Early on they used only a guitar and their voices to imitate a whole band.
They recorded with Louis Armstrong and Bing Crosby.
Paper Doll was one of the biggest hits of the 1940s.
songs: You Always Hurt the One You Love

influencedBy.why: They recorded with Armstrong, and their horn-like vocal phrasing comes from jazz players like him.
They appeared with Crosby on record and radio early in their career.

influenced.why: The Ink Spots followed the Mills Brothers into pop vocal harmony.
Their smooth group harmony fed the sound of late 1940s R&B groups.
Martin named Harry Mills as a key influence on his singing.

cousins.why: Rhythmic close harmony with voices doing an instrument's work.
Family harmony with a light, swinging touch.

summary: The Andrews Sisters were a vocal trio whose tight, swinging harmonies made them the top female group of the swing era. Their songs became part of the sound of the World War II years.
know: Bei Mir Bist Du Schön, a Yiddish song, was their breakthrough in 1937.
They recorded many duets with Bing Crosby.
Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy was featured in the 1941 film Buck Privates.
songs: Don't Sit Under the Apple Tree

influencedBy.why: They worked with Crosby on dozens of recordings.
Their swing arrangements came from the big band sound Miller and others made popular.

influenced.why: The Pointer Sisters' early nostalgic swing harmonies drew on the Andrews Sisters' style.
Aguilera's Candyman was modeled on Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy.

cousins.why: A polished female vocal group that defined the pop sound of its time.
Family harmonies that carried a whole era's mood.

summary: Al Jolson was a singer and entertainer who was among the most popular performers of the early 20th century. He starred in The Jazz Singer, the first feature film with synchronized singing and dialogue.
know: The Jazz Singer in 1927 marked the start of the sound film era.
His recording of Gershwin's Swanee made it a huge hit in 1920.
He was known for his big, emotional stage style and direct connection to an audience.
songs: Rock-a-Bye Your Baby with a Dixie Melody

influencedBy.why: Gershwin wrote Swanee, which became Jolson's signature hit.
Jolson's song choices came largely from Tin Pan Alley writers like Berlin.

influenced.why: Crosby named Jolson as an early idol before developing his own quieter style.
Wilson recorded a full tribute album to Jolson, You Ain't Heard Nothin' Yet.
Lewis named Jolson among his main early influences as a showman.

cousins.why: An all-out showman who sang to the back row.
A total entertainer who made every performance an event.

summary: Irving Berlin was a songwriter whose simple, memorable melodies helped define American popular song. He wrote hundreds of hits across more than half a century, many of them now standards.
know: Alexander's Ragtime Band in 1911 was his first major hit.
White Christmas, sung by Bing Crosby, became one of the best selling singles ever.
He could play piano in only one key and used a special transposing piano.
keyAlbums: Annie Get Your Gun (Original Broadway Cast)
songs: There's No Business Like Show Business

influencedBy.why: Berlin's early hits rode the ragtime craze that Joplin's music had helped start.

influenced.why: Gershwin admired Berlin deeply and considered him the model American songwriter.
Crosby's recordings of Berlin songs, above all White Christmas, were central to his career.
Ella recorded a full Irving Berlin Song Book in 1958.
Berlin songs are a large part of the standard repertoire Sinatra drew from.

cousins.why: Songwriters who turned out simple, unforgettable hits for decades.
A songwriter's songwriter with a plain style and a sharp eye.

summary: George Gershwin was a composer who joined popular song, jazz and concert music. His songs and Rhapsody in Blue became cornerstones of American music, and Porgy and Bess is a landmark opera.
know: Rhapsody in Blue premiered in 1924 with Paul Whiteman's orchestra.
He wrote most of his songs with his brother Ira, who wrote the lyrics.
The chords of I Got Rhythm became one of the most used frameworks in jazz.

influencedBy.why: Gershwin saw Berlin as the great model of American songwriting.
Gershwin spent time with the Harlem stride pianists and drew on their style.
His early piano work came out of the ragtime tradition Joplin led.

influenced.why: Ella recorded a full George and Ira Gershwin Song Book.
The I Got Rhythm chord pattern became a core framework for bebop tunes.
Davis and Gil Evans recorded a full orchestral version of Porgy and Bess.
Evans arranged Porgy and Bess for Miles Davis.
Her first hit was I Loves You, Porgy, from Porgy and Bess.
Her version of Summertime with Big Brother and the Holding Company is one of her best known.

cousins.why: A composer who wrote long-form works that blurred jazz and concert music.
Blended popular dance music with classical forms.

summary: Cole Porter was a songwriter known for witty lyrics and sophisticated melodies. He wrote both words and music, and his songs remain central to the American songbook.
know: Unlike many songwriters of his era, he wrote both music and lyrics.
Anything Goes and Kiss Me, Kate were among his biggest shows.
His list songs packed in clever rhymes and cultural references.
songs: I Get a Kick Out of You
I've Got You Under My Skin

influencedBy.why: Porter worked in the songwriting world Berlin had defined and admired his craft.

influenced.why: The Cole Porter Song Book in 1956 was the first of Ella's famous songbook albums.
I've Got You Under My Skin became one of Sinatra's signature recordings.
Bennett recorded the Porter album Love for Sale with Lady Gaga in 2021.
Gaga recorded the Cole Porter album Love for Sale with Tony Bennett.

cousins.why: A songwriter whose wit and irony live in the lyric.
Clever wordplay and rhymes put to good tunes.

summary: Peggy Lee was a singer and songwriter famous for a cool, understated delivery. Her version of Fever and her songwriting made her one of the most respected pop vocalists of her era.
know: She first became known singing with Benny Goodman's band.
She co-wrote songs for Disney's Lady and the Tramp and voiced several characters.
Her 1958 Fever was a cover of a Little Willie John hit.

influencedBy.why: Lee named Holiday as a model for her relaxed, behind-the-beat phrasing.
She learned as a band singer with Goodman in the early 1940s.
Lee credited the Basie band's restraint as an example of saying more with less.
She covered his Fever and made it her signature song.

influenced.why: Madonna covered Fever in 1993, drawing on Lee's version.
lang has named Lee among her influences in torch and pop singing.
Beyoncé recorded Fever, following Lee's arrangement.

cousins.why: Warm, controlled torch singing with huge feeling held back.
Cool, smoky, understated delivery.

summary: Les Paul was a guitarist and inventor who pioneered multitrack recording and the solid-body electric guitar. His hits with Mary Ford used layered guitars and voices in ways no one had heard before.
know: The Gibson Les Paul guitar is named after him.
He developed sound-on-sound and multitrack tape techniques.
How High the Moon with Mary Ford was a number one hit in 1951.

influencedBy.why: Paul said Reinhardt's fast, melodic guitar inspired him.
His jazz electric guitar grew alongside Christian's single-note style.
Crosby backed his recording work and gave him an early Ampex tape machine.

influenced.why: Atkins admired Paul and the two made the album Chester & Lester together.
Beck made a full tribute show and album to Les Paul's music.
Their studio layering of parts builds on the multitrack methods Paul pioneered.
Brian May's stacked guitar orchestrations follow Paul's layered-guitar approach.

cousins.why: A sound pioneer who built new music out of tape tricks.
Used the studio as an instrument to create sounds no one had heard.

summary: Dean Martin was a singer, actor and comedian known for a relaxed, easygoing crooning style. He had a string of pop hits in the 1950s and 1960s and was a central member of the Rat Pack.
know: He first became famous in a comedy duo with Jerry Lewis.
Everybody Loves Somebody knocked the Beatles from number one in 1964.
He hosted a long-running TV variety show from 1965 to 1974.
songs: Ain't That a Kick in the Head

influencedBy.why: Martin modeled his relaxed crooning on Crosby.
Martin named Harry Mills of the Mills Brothers as a key vocal influence.

influenced.why: Elvis admired Martin and his ballad singing.

cousins.why: Smooth, unhurried singing that makes it sound easy.
A velvet baritone that never pushes.

summary: Tony Bennett was a singer who kept the Great American Songbook alive for more than seven decades. He moved easily between pop hits and jazz, and late in life found new audiences through duets.
know: I Left My Heart in San Francisco became his signature song in 1962.
He made two duet albums with pianist Bill Evans.
His MTV Unplugged album won the Grammy for Album of the Year.
keyAlbums: I Left My Heart in San Francisco
songs: I Left My Heart in San Francisco
The Best Is Yet to Come

influencedBy.why: Sinatra championed Bennett, and his phrasing set the standard Bennett worked within.
Bennett grew up listening to Crosby and named him an early model.
Bennett named Armstrong as a key influence on his jazz feel.
Bennett credited Holiday for her phrasing and honesty.
Bennett said he learned phrasing by listening to instrumentalists like Tatum.
Bennett made two albums with the Basie band in 1958 and 1959.

influenced.why: Gaga made two jazz duet albums with Bennett, Cheek to Cheek and Love for Sale.
Winehouse admired Bennett and recorded Body and Soul with him in 2011.
lang made the duet album A Wonderful World with Bennett.

cousins.why: Took the standards seriously and sang them for decades.
Moved between genres while keeping a deep feel for a song.

summary: The Orioles were a vocal group led by Sonny Til whose ballads helped create the doo-wop sound. Their success started a wave of R&B groups named after birds.
know: It's Too Soon to Know in 1948 was one of the first R&B vocal group hits.
Their 1953 Crying in the Chapel crossed over to the pop charts.
Sonny Til's emotional lead singing was widely copied.
songs: What Are You Doing New Year's Eve

influencedBy.why: The Orioles' ballad style grew straight from the Ink Spots' tenor-led sound.
Their smooth harmonies follow the Mills Brothers' pop vocal model.

influenced.why: The Moonglows were among the many 1950s groups that followed the Orioles' ballad formula.
Their slow, lead-tenor ballads extend the path the Orioles cut.
The New York street-corner groups of the 1950s built on the Orioles' model.

cousins.why: Rich, stacked group harmony around a sweet lead.
Tight, high harmonies that ache.

summary: The Dominoes were a vocal group run by Billy Ward whose gospel-charged leads helped push R&B toward rock and roll and soul. They launched the careers of Clyde McPhatter and Jackie Wilson.
know: Billy Ward was a trained musician who coached and managed the group.
Clyde McPhatter sang lead on their early hits before leaving to form the Drifters.
Jackie Wilson replaced McPhatter as lead singer.

influencedBy.why: Their lead-and-bass vocal group setup came from the Ink Spots' pattern.
The Orioles' R&B ballads were the immediate model for groups like the Dominoes.
Their gospel-style rhythm singing draws on quartets like the Golden Gate Quartet.

influenced.why: McPhatter developed his gospel-style lead singing as the Dominoes' frontman.
McPhatter took the Dominoes' sound with him when he formed the Drifters.
Wilson learned his trade as the Dominoes' lead singer before going solo.

cousins.why: Gospel quartet singing with a charged, star lead.
Church-rooted harmony that crossed over to the pop world.

summary: The Drifters were a vocal group whose changing lineup produced hits for over two decades. Their records with Leiber and Stoller added strings and Latin rhythms to R&B and shaped 1960s pop production.
know: Clyde McPhatter formed the group in 1953.
There Goes My Baby in 1959 was one of the first R&B hits with strings.
Ben E. King sang lead on There Goes My Baby and Save the Last Dance for Me.
keyAlbums: Save the Last Dance for Me
songs: Save the Last Dance for Me

influencedBy.why: McPhatter founded the group and set its gospel-flavored lead style.
The early Drifters carried over the Dominoes' sound through McPhatter.
Leiber and Stoller produced and wrote their late 1950s hits.
Ertegun signed the group to Atlantic and guided their early records.
